prompt: A whole number written in the source, such as `42`, has which type?
hint: It is one of the two defaults.

choices.text: `long`, because it is the safest
choices.why: A plain whole number is an `int`; `long` needs the suffix `L`.

choices.text: `int`
choices.why: Right: and a number with a point is a `double`.

choices.text: Whichever is smallest that fits, here `byte`
choices.why: Java does not shrink a literal to fit; `42` is an `int` whatever its size.

choices.text: The type of the variable it is put into
choices.why: `8_000_000_000` into a `long` failed for exactly this reason: the literal is typed first.

prompt: How many bits does an `int` take?
hint: `Integer.SIZE` printed it.

prompt: `Overflow` printed `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1`. What came out, and why?
hint: Java does not stop at the largest value.

choices.text: `2147483648`, because Java widens the result to a `long`
choices.why: That is what the `long` version printed; the `int` sum stays an `int`.

choices.text: `-2147483648`: it wrapped round to the smallest `int`, silently
choices.why: Right: no error, no warning, and that is the danger.

choices.text: An `ArithmeticException` saying the value overflowed
choices.why: Plain arithmetic never throws on overflow; lesson 8's `Math.addExact` does.

choices.text: `2147483647` again, because the value is capped at the maximum
choices.why: There is no cap: it went past the end and came round the other side.

prompt: `long people = 8_000_000_000;` does not compile. What is the smallest fix?
hint: The literal's type is decided before the variable is looked at.

choices.text: Remove the underscores
choices.why: The underscores are ignored by the compiler; the number is still too large for an `int`.

choices.text: Declare `people` as `double` instead
choices.why: The literal is read as an `int` before the variable's type matters, so it fails the same way.

choices.text: Add the suffix: `8_000_000_000L`
choices.why: Right: the `L` makes the literal a `long`.

prompt: A web shop stores each product's total page views in an `int`. One product has been viewed 2,147,483,647 times. What happens at the next view?
hint: That number is a familiar one.

choices.text: The program stops with an error the shop's logs will show
choices.why: Overflow raises nothing; there is no error for a log to show.

choices.text: The count becomes -2,147,483,648, and nothing reports it
choices.why: Right: it is `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, and one more wraps it to the smallest `int`.

choices.text: The count stays at 2,147,483,647 from then on
choices.why: Nothing caps an `int`; it wraps.

choices.text: Java moves the value into a `long` the first time it is needed
choices.why: Java never changes a variable's type; it was decided at compile time.

prompt: `char letter = 'A';` and then `letter++;`. What does `System.out.println(letter)` print?
hint: A `char` is a number underneath.

choices.why: That is what `letter + 0` would print after the increment; printed as a `char` it is a letter.
Right: the code 65 became 66, which is `B`.
That would be joining text; `++` adds one to the number.

choices.text: Nothing: `++` is a compile error on a `char`
choices.why: It compiled and ran in `Overflow`.

prompt: Match each literal to its type.
hint: The suffix and the quotes decide.

prompt: Why does Java need `Integer` when it already has `int`?
hint: Think of what the collections hold.

choices.text: Because `Integer` can hold larger numbers than `int`
choices.why: It holds exactly an `int`'s range; the wrapper adds an object around it, not bits.

choices.text: Because much of Java works with objects only, such as the collections
choices.why: Right: a list of numbers is a list of `Integer`.

choices.text: Because arithmetic on `int` is slower than on `Integer`
choices.why: The reverse: arithmetic on `Integer` unboxes to `int` first.

prompt: `Integer a = 127, b = 127;` gives `a == b` true, and `Integer c = 128, d = 128;` gives `c == d` false. What explains the difference?
hint: `==` on objects compares references.

choices.text: 128 does not fit in a byte, so it is stored with less precision
choices.why: Both are `int` values stored exactly; precision is not involved.

choices.text: `==` compares values up to 127 and references above it
choices.why: `==` always compares references on objects; the values just happened to share an object.

choices.text: Boxing reuses cached objects from -128 to 127, so `a` and `b` are one object
choices.why: Right: 128 is outside the cache, so `c` and `d` are two objects.

prompt: Two `Integer` variables hold the same value. Which comparison is right whatever the value?
hint: The section's rule for objects.

choices.text: `x.equals(y)`
choices.why: Right: it compares the values, and said `true` for 128.
It compares references, and said `false` for two boxed 128s.

choices.text: `x == y`, as long as both were assigned from literals
choices.why: Literals are where the cache came in: 127 passed and 128 failed.

prompt: Turning an `int` into an `Integer` automatically is called ___, and taking the `int` back out is called unboxing.
hint: The opposite of the other word.

prompt: `int copies = copiesLeft;` throws a `NullPointerException` that mentions `intValue()`, and the line has no method call. Where did the call come from?
hint: Someone wrote the conversion for you.

choices.text: From the JVM, which checks every assignment for `null`
choices.why: The JVM checks nothing extra; it ran a call that was in the bytecode.

choices.text: The compiler wrote it, to unbox the `Integer` into an `int`
choices.why: Right: unboxing is a call to `intValue()`, and calling it on `null` fails.

choices.text: From `System.out.println` on the next line
choices.why: The stack trace names line 5, the assignment, before anything was printed.

prompt: The first run named the null variable `<local1>`, and the second named it `copiesLeft`. What changed?
hint: The second run was compiled differently.

choices.text: The second run used Java 21, which prints names
choices.why: Both ran on 25; the class file was what differed.

choices.text: The variable was renamed between the runs
choices.why: The same `Missing.java` was used both times.

choices.text: `javac -g` kept local variable names in the class file
choices.why: Right: without them the JVM can only number the locals.

prompt: `var year = 1899;` What is the type of `year`?
hint: The literal decides.

choices.text: None: `var` variables have no type
choices.why: They have one, written by the compiler; `/vars` printed it.

choices.text: `int`
choices.why: Right: a plain whole number is an `int`.

choices.text: `long`, since years can grow
choices.why: Only `1899L` would be a `long`.

choices.text: `Integer`, since `var` makes objects
choices.why: `var` infers the literal's type, a primitive here.

prompt: Which of these lines does the compiler refuse? Choose all that apply.
hint: The type is decided once, from the value at the declaration.

choices.text: `var title;`
choices.why: Yes: no value, nothing to infer from.

choices.text: `var author = null;`
choices.why: Yes: `null` has no type of its own.

choices.text: `var initial = 'D';`
choices.why: No: it is a `char`, as `/vars` showed.

choices.text: `year = "nineteenth century";` after `var year = 1899;`
choices.why: Yes: `year` is an `int`, and stays one.

prompt: Where does the section say `var` costs the reader something?
hint: The reader needs the type from somewhere.

choices.text: `var members = new java.util.ArrayList<String>();`
choices.why: There the type is on the same line, so `var` saves writing it twice.

choices.text: `var total = calculate();`
choices.why: Right: nothing on the line says whether `total` is an `int`, a `long` or a `double`.

choices.text: `var title = "Dom Casmurro";`
choices.why: The quotes make the `String` plain to every reader.

prompt: Where can `var` be used?
hint: Fields and parameters are read by other code.

choices.text: Anywhere a type is written
choices.why: Not for fields, parameters or return types, which are always written out.

choices.text: For fields of a class, so the class is shorter
choices.why: Fields keep their written types; `var` is for locals.

choices.text: For local variables, inside a method, with a value
choices.why: Right: and only where that value gives the compiler a type.

prompt: A library counts the milliseconds since 1970 in a variable. Which type, and why?
hint: How many milliseconds are there in fifty years?

choices.text: `int`, because it is the default for whole numbers
choices.why: The default overflows here: two billion milliseconds is under a month.

choices.text: `double`, because time is a measurement
choices.why: Milliseconds are whole, and a `double` would round large values.

choices.text: `long`, because the count passes two billion
choices.why: Right: it is the section's own example of a value that outgrows an `int`.

prompt: A method returns `Integer` and gives back `null` when a book is not found. The caller writes `int stock = findStock(isbn);`. What happens for a missing book?
hint: The assignment unboxes.

choices.text: `stock` becomes 0, the default for an `int`
choices.why: There is no default here: unboxing `null` throws before anything is assigned.

choices.text: A `NullPointerException` on that line
choices.why: Right: the unboxing calls `intValue()` on `null`.

choices.text: A compile error, because `null` cannot become an `int`
choices.why: The compiler cannot know the method returns `null`; it fails at run time.

choices.text: `stock` holds `null` until a value is known
choices.why: An `int` cannot hold `null` at all.
